lead: Every element a browser draws is a rectangle, and CSS builds that rectangle from four layers. Content sits in the middle. Padding adds space inside the border, the border draws the visible edge, and the margin pushes neighbours away. The browser adds these widths to find how much room the element really takes. That is why a box declared 300px wide can render wider, and why one declaration, box-sizing, changes the arithmetic.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.5 for selectors, units and the cascade, and Chapter 2.2 for the elements being boxed.

blocks.text: Every element generates a rectangular box. CSS describes that box as four layers, one inside the next. From the outside in they are margin, border, padding and content. Picture a framed photograph with a mat around it and empty wall space around the frame.

The content box holds the element's text, image or child boxes. The width and height properties size this content box, not the whole visible box. An element declared width: 300px has 300px of content space before anything else is added.

Padding is space inside the border, between the border and the content. It takes the element's background colour, so it looks like part of the element. It cannot be negative. The four sides are set with padding-top, padding-right, padding-bottom and padding-left.
The border is the visible edge around the padding. It has three parts: width, style and colour. If the style is none, nothing is drawn even when a width is given.
The margin is transparent space outside the border. It separates the element from its neighbours. Margin can be negative, which pulls neighbours closer or makes boxes overlap.
rendered width = width + padding-left + padding-right + border-left-width + border-right-width
blocks.where: width is the content width in px under the default content-box; padding and border widths are lengths in px.

blocks.text: Margins are added on top when we ask how much room the element blocks out: outer width = rendered width + margin-left + margin-right. Background and border stop at the border edge; margins are always transparent.

The default surprises beginners. Declare width: 300px, add padding: 20px and border: 5px, and the browser draws a box 350px wide. The width measured only the content. This is box-sizing: content-box, the initial value.

Designers often set box-sizing: border-box on every element. Then a declared width includes padding and border, and the content shrinks to fit: content width = declared width − left/right padding − left/right border. Margins stay outside. This makes percentage widths and side-by-side layouts predictable.
The padding and margin shorthands take one to four values, running clockwise from the top.

head: Shorthand
Result
rows: top, right, bottom, left in that order

blocks.text: Border shorthands follow the same idea. border: 2px dashed #333 sets width, style and colour in one declaration, and the style is mandatory for a visible line. Sides have their own properties, such as border-top-width. border-radius: 8px rounds the corners; a square with border-radius: 50% becomes a circle.
An outline is drawn outside the border. It takes no space in layout and does not change the box size. Browsers use it for the focus ring on links and buttons.

margin: auto on a block element with a fixed width shares the leftover horizontal space equally, centring the box. It works only when the element is narrower than its container; without a width the block fills the line and there is nothing to share.
Negative margins are legal. margin-left: -20px pulls the element 20px left, over its neighbour. They are used for overlapping cards and for closing gaps, but they make layout harder to reason about.

Vertical margins of two stacked block boxes collapse. If one has margin-bottom: 24px and the next has margin-top: 16px, the gap between them is 24px, the larger value, not 40px. Parent and child margins can collapse too when no border, padding or content separates them. Horizontal margins never collapse.

display decides how a box treats width and vertical margins. A block box starts on a new line, fills the available width and respects width, height and all margins. An inline box sits in a line of text; width and height are ignored and vertical margins do not push lines apart. inline-block sits in the line like inline content but is sized like a block, which suits buttons and small cards.

When content is larger than its box, overflow decides what happens. visible lets it spill out, hidden clips it, scroll always shows scrollbars and auto shows them only when needed. Prefer auto for text panels.

figure.caption: The margin is transparent and sits outside the visible edge. Here the border, padding and content give a rendered width of 350px, and the margins make the total space 370px.

spec.aria: Four nested layers from outside in: a 10px transparent margin, a 5px solid border, 20px of padding, and the 300px content box.

examples.question: A card is styled with width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid black; margin: 10px. The page uses the default box-sizing. (a) Find the rendered width of the card and the horizontal space it blocks out, margins included. (b) The stylesheet then adds box-sizing: border-box to the card, with width still 300px. Find the new content width.
steps: Default box-sizing is content-box, so the content width is 300px.
Space blocked out = rendered width + left and right margin = 350 + 10 + 10 = 370px.
With border-box, the declared 300px includes padding and border: content width = 300 − 40 − 10 = 250px.
examples.answer: The card renders 350px wide and blocks out 370px; with border-box its content width becomes 250px.
examples.check:
w = 300
pad = 20
bd = 5
mar = 10
rendered = w + 2 * pad + 2 * bd
outer = rendered + 2 * mar
content_bb = w - 2 * pad - 2 * bd
print(rendered)
print(outer)
print(content_bb)

traps: Treating width: 300px as the final box width. By default padding and border sit outside it, so the rendered width is 350px.
Adding collapsed margins. Two stacked blocks with margins 24px and 16px have a 24px gap, not 40px.
Writing border-width without border-style. No style means no visible border.
Expecting margin: auto to centre anything. It needs a block-level box with a set width; inline boxes and full-width blocks do not centre.
Assuming padding can be negative. Only margins accept negative values.

quiz.q: Name the four layers of the CSS box model from outside in.
What is the initial value of box-sizing?
An element has width: 200px, padding: 15px and border: 5px, with default box-sizing. Why does it render 240px wide?
quiz.a: width sizes only the content, 200px. Padding adds 15 + 15 = 30px and the border adds 5 + 5 = 10px, so the rendered width is 240px.

quiz.q: An element has width: 250px, padding: 10px, border: 2px and margin: 8px, with content-box. Find its rendered width and the horizontal space it blocks out.
An element has width: 400px, padding: 25px, border: 3px and box-sizing: border-box. Find its content width.
Two stacked paragraphs have margin-bottom: 24px and margin-top: 16px. What gap appears between them, and why?
quiz.a: 24px. Adjacent vertical margins collapse and the larger margin wins; they are not added.

quiz.q: State one difference between an outline and a border.
quiz.a: An outline is drawn outside the border and takes no space in layout, so it does not change the box size; a border takes space and affects the rendered box.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production CSS, resets almost always set box-sizing: border-box globally, and browser DevTools show the box model as a coloured diagram when you inspect an element. Modern CSS adds logical properties such as margin-inline-start and padding-block, which map to left/right or top/bottom depending on writing direction, so the same rule works for Arabic or Hindi layouts. Search for "CSS logical properties", "MDN box model" and "CSS box-sizing" to go further.
